lessons.title: Group Structures, Holding Companies and Cross-Holdings

body.text: In a business group, the listed company you own is one node in a web. Value can travel along every line of that web, and it does not always travel towards you.

children.text: Much of corporate India is organised as business groups: a family or holding entity controlling several companies, some listed on NSE and BSE, many unlisted, often holding stakes in each other. The structure can be perfectly sensible. It can also be the plumbing through which cash quietly moves from the company you own into companies you do not. Promoter holding and pledges tell you about the promoter's stake in your company. Group structure tells you what else the promoter owns, and where their real economic interest lies.

body.caption: Group structures you will meet in Indian listed companies

cells: Listed parent with subsidiaries
Your company owns operating subsidiaries, joint ventures, and associates
Are subsidiaries creating value, or absorbing the parent's cash through loans and guarantees?
Unlisted holding company on top
A private promoter entity holds controlling stakes in several listed group companies
Does the unlisted holdco need cash that the listed companies are pressured to supply?
Pyramid
Promoter controls Company A, which controls Company B, which controls Company C
Does the promoter have an incentive to move value up the chain towards the companies it owns more of?
Cross-holdings
Group companies own shares in each other
Is the same capital being counted twice, and are group companies propping up each other's share prices?
Listed holding company
A listed entity whose main assets are stakes in other group companies
Why does it trade at a steep discount to the value of what it owns?

markDefs.definition: The gap between the voting control a promoter exercises over a company and the share of its profits the promoter actually owns. The bigger the wedge, the bigger the temptation to shift value elsewhere.

children.text: In a pyramid, a promoter needs only a controlling stake at each layer to control every company below it. But the promoter's economic interest, their share of each company's profits, shrinks at every step. The difference between control and economic interest is called the
, and it is the single most useful idea for thinking about group governance.

body.latex: \text{Promoter's Economic Interest in Bottom Company} = s_1 \times s_2 \times \dots \times s_n
body.caption: Multiply the stake held at each layer of the chain

children.text: Say a promoter owns 51% of Company A, A owns 51% of Company B, B owns 51% of Company C, and C owns 51% of Company D. The promoter controls all four with a majority at every level. Their economic interest, though, is 51% in A, 51% × 51% = 26.01% in B, 13.27% in C, and just 6.77% in D.

body.title: Control vs economic interest down a 51% pyramid

markDefs.definition: Moving value out of a company to benefit its controlling shareholder, through related party sales or purchases at unfair prices, loans, guarantees, or asset transfers.

children.text: Now think like a promoter with weak ethics. Every ₹100 crore of profit that stays in Company D is worth ₹6.77 crore to them. Move that ₹100 crore up to Company A, through an overpriced purchase, a cheap asset sale, or a loan that never gets repaid, and it is worth ₹51 crore to them. The minority shareholders of D pay for it. This is called
, and pyramids create the motive for it. They do not prove it happens, but they tell you exactly where to look.

body.title: Calculate the Wedge
body.prompt: A promoter family owns 70% of an unlisted holding company. The holding company owns 55% of Listed Company X. Listed Company X owns 60% of Listed Company Y. What is the promoter family's economic interest in Company Y? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 0.70 × 0.55 × 0.60 = 0.231, or 23.1%. The family controls Company Y through a 60% stake at the level directly above it, but owns only 23.1% of its profits. A shareholder in Y should watch closely for transactions between Y and X or the holding company, where the family's interest is higher.

body.text: When you own a company low in a pyramid, the question to ask about every related party transaction is simple: which direction is the value moving? Value flowing up the chain, towards entities the promoter owns more of, deserves the most scrutiny.

children.text: Legitimate Structure vs Complexity as Camouflage

Many subsidiaries exist for good reasons. RBI and IRDAI require banking, lending, and insurance businesses to sit in separately regulated entities. Joint venture partners want their own company. Overseas operations need local entities. None of that is a red flag. The warning sign is complexity that the business does not explain.

columns.label: Explainable
points: Subsidiaries required by regulation, such as a separate NBFC or insurance arm
Joint ventures with named, credible partners
Overseas subsidiaries in countries where the company actually sells
Subsidiary count stable, with each entity's purpose clear from the annual report

columns.label: Warning Signs
points: Dozens of small subsidiaries with no clear business purpose
Entities in low-tax jurisdictions unrelated to the company's markets
Frequent creation, merger, or striking off of subsidiaries
Loans, investments, or guarantees to group companies that are not even subsidiaries

children.text: IL&FS is the reminder of what complexity can hide. When the infrastructure lender began defaulting in September 2018, investigators had to untangle a group of more than 300 entities, including many step-down subsidiaries and overseas companies, carrying group debt of over ₹90,000 crore. The government superseded its board on 1 October 2018. The sheer number of entities made it very hard for lenders, rating agencies, and investors to see where the debt sat and which entities could actually service it.

body.label: Companies (Restriction on Number of Layers) Rules, 2017
body.context: Most Indian companies cannot hold investments through more than two layers of subsidiaries. Banks, NBFCs, insurers, government companies, and subsidiaries set up abroad under local law are among the exceptions.

children.text: Standalone vs Consolidated: The Two-Minute Group Check

Screener.in lets you toggle between standalone and consolidated financials. Standalone shows the listed company alone. Consolidated adds its subsidiaries and its share of joint ventures and associates. The gap between the two tells you what the rest of the group is doing to your company's numbers.

body.caption: What the standalone to consolidated gap tells you

cells: Consolidated profit well above standalone
Subsidiaries are profitable and add value
Whether the parent can actually access that profit through dividends, or it stays trapped
Consolidated profit persistently below standalone
Subsidiaries are loss-making and dragging the group down
How the losses are funded: parent loans, equity infusions, or guarantees
Consolidated debt far above standalone debt
Borrowing is parked in subsidiaries
Whether the parent has guaranteed that debt, making it your problem
Standalone 'investments' or 'loans to subsidiaries' growing every year
Parent cash is steadily moving into the group
Returns earned on those investments, and whether any have been written down

body.title: Read the Gap
body.question: A listed company reports standalone net profit of ₹480 crore and consolidated net profit of ₹290 crore for the same year. This pattern has repeated for four years. Its standalone balance sheet shows loans to subsidiaries rising every year. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Consolidated accounts are always less reliable than standalone accounts
The parent's subsidiaries are losing money, and the parent is funding those losses with its own cash
The company is hiding profits in its subsidiaries to reduce tax
There is nothing to analyse, because the difference is only an accounting presentation
body.explanation: A consistent ₹190 crore gap means the subsidiaries together lose money year after year, and rising loans to subsidiaries show the parent is financing them. As a shareholder in the parent, you are paying for those losses. The next question is whether those subsidiaries have a credible path to profit, or whether this is a long-running drain.

children.text: Listed Holding Companies and Their Discount

Some groups have a listed company whose main assets are stakes in other group companies. Listed holding companies such as Bajaj Holdings & Investment and Tata Investment Corporation have historically traded well below the market value of the shares they hold. This holding company discount is partly a governance discount: minority shareholders in the holdco have no say over when, or whether, that value is ever passed on to them.

body.latex: \text{Holding Company Discount} = 1 - \frac{\text{Market Cap of Holdco}}{\text{Value of Stakes Held} + \text{Other Net Assets}}
body.caption: The denominator is the holdco's net asset value (NAV)

headers: Why It Lowers the Holdco's Value

cells: No control over distribution
The holdco rarely sells stakes or passes through all dividends, so NAV is not something shareholders can realise
Tax leakage
Dividends and any eventual sale of stakes can be taxed at the holdco level before reaching its shareholders
Capital allocation risk
Cash at the holdco can be redeployed into group companies that need support, not the best opportunities
Liquidity and extra costs
Holdcos are often thinly traded and carry their own layer of expenses

children.text: A deep holdco discount is not automatically a bargain. It narrows only if something changes the reasons above, such as a buyback, a higher dividend payout, a demerger, or a restructuring that hands the underlying shares to holdco shareholders.
Where to Map the Group Yourself

body.caption: Documents that reveal the group structure

cells: Form AOC-1
Annexure to the annual report
Every subsidiary, associate, and joint venture with key financials such as capital, net worth, turnover, and profit
Related party disclosures (Ind AS 24)
Notes to the financial statements
The full list of related parties, including promoter group entities that are not subsidiaries, and transactions with each
Shareholding pattern
BSE and NSE filings, quarterly
Every promoter group entity holding shares in the listed company, by name
Contingent liabilities note
Notes to the financial statements
Corporate guarantees given on behalf of subsidiaries and other group companies
Standalone vs consolidated toggle
Company page on screener.in
The combined effect of subsidiaries on profit, debt, and cash flow

body.text: Corporate guarantees are one of the least-read numbers in an annual report. A guarantee for a group company's loan does not appear as debt on your company's balance sheet, but if that group company defaults, the lender comes to your company for payment. Always compare total guarantees given with your company's net worth.

body.title: The Company With 42 Subsidiaries
body.scenario: A mid cap engineering company listed on NSE has a net worth of ₹2,000 crore. Its AOC-1 lists 42 subsidiaries and step-down subsidiaries, including 11 incorporated in Mauritius, Singapore, and the British Virgin Islands, although the company earns over 90% of its revenue in India. Consolidated profit has been below standalone profit for five straight years. The contingent liabilities note shows corporate guarantees of ₹1,200 crore given on behalf of 'group companies', several of which are owned by the promoter family and are not subsidiaries of the listed company.
body.prompt: What does this structure tell you about risk to minority shareholders? Which numbers matter most, and why?
body.modelAnswer: The most important number is the ₹1,200 crore of guarantees, equal to 60% of net worth, given for promoter-owned entities the listed company does not even own. If those entities default, lenders can claim against the listed company, so minority shareholders are underwriting the promoter's private businesses with no share of their upside. Second, 11 offshore entities for a business that earns over 90% of revenue in India have no obvious commercial purpose, which raises the question of whether they exist to move money rather than to do business. Third, five years of consolidated profit below standalone means the subsidiaries are a persistent drain funded by the parent. Individually each point needs explanation; together they describe a structure where value can easily flow from the listed company to the promoter group. Before investing, you would want the guarantees explained and reduced, the purpose of each offshore entity disclosed, and a path to profitability for the subsidiaries.

cards.definition: A chain of control where the promoter controls Company A, A controls B, and so on, gaining control of lower companies with a shrinking economic stake.
The gap between a promoter's voting control and their economic interest in a company.
Shifting value out of a company, typically to entities where the controlling shareholder has a larger economic interest.
A subsidiary of a subsidiary, one or more layers below the listed parent.
The gap between a holding company's market cap and the value of the assets it holds, expressed as a percentage of that value.
The statement attached to the annual report summarising the financials of every subsidiary, associate, and joint venture.
A promise by a company to repay another entity's loan if it defaults. Disclosed as a contingent liability, not as debt.

body.title: Map the Group Behind One of Your Holdings
steps: Open the latest annual report from the Documents section on screener.in and find Form AOC-1; count the subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures
Note any entities in countries where the company has no meaningful business, and any with negative net worth
Toggle screener.in between standalone and consolidated and compare net profit and borrowings for the last five years
In the related party note, list the promoter group entities that are not subsidiaries but still transact with the company
In the contingent liabilities note, add up corporate guarantees for group companies and divide by the company's net worth

If the promoter controls your company through other entities, multiply the stakes along the chain to estimate the promoter's economic interest, and note which related entities the promoter owns more of

body.text: Companies named in this lesson illustrate group and holding structures and are used for education only, based on public filings and widely reported events. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: In a business group, your listed company is one node in a web, and value can flow along every link
In a pyramid, economic interest is the product of stakes at each layer, so control can far exceed ownership; a 51% chain four layers deep leaves just 6.77% economic interest
The wedge between control and ownership creates the motive for tunnelling value up the chain, so scrutinise transactions that move value towards entities the promoter owns more of
Regulated or commercially logical subsidiaries are normal; unexplained complexity, offshore entities, and guarantees for non-subsidiary group companies are not
Compare standalone and consolidated numbers on screener.in, and read Form AOC-1, the related party note, and the contingent liabilities note to map the group
Listed holding companies often trade at large discounts to NAV, which narrow only if something changes how value reaches holdco shareholders
